questions.explain: The threads of a warp execute the same instruction on their own data. That is why threads that branch differently cost time, and why block sizes are chosen as multiples of 32.

questions.q: The threads of one warp take different sides of an if. What does the hardware do?
options: It follows the side most of the threads chose
It runs one side and then the other, with the threads that are not on that side idle each time
It splits the warp into two smaller warps for the rest of the kernel
It stops the kernel with an error
questions.explain: A warp has one instruction stream. Both branches are executed and each thread is masked off for the one it did not take, so heavy branching inside a kernel wastes much of the device.

questions.q: You time a PyTorch operation on the GPU with a clock reading before and after, and it appears to take almost no time. Why?
options: The clock of the processor stops while the GPU works
PyTorch caches the result of earlier calls
The GPU really is that fast for every operation
GPU calls return before the work is done; call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading the clock
questions.explain: Launching a kernel only queues it. Without a synchronise you measure the launch, and the real cost lands on whichever later line happens to wait for the result.

questions.q: What does pin_memory=True do in a PyTorch DataLoader?
options: Keeps the whole data set in GPU memory
Fixes the order of the batches between epochs
Stops the operating system from using the GPU for anything else
Keeps batches in page-locked host memory, so the copy to the GPU is faster and can run in the background
questions.explain: Ordinary memory can be moved or swapped out, so it must be staged before a transfer. Page-locked memory can be copied to the device directly, and non_blocking=True then lets training continue during the copy.

questions.q: Two MPI processes each call a blocking MPI_Recv from the other, and only afterwards an MPI_Send. What happens?
options: MPI swaps the order of the calls
A deadlock: each waits for a message the other has not sent yet
The process with the lower rank goes first
The messages cross and both continue
questions.explain: A blocking receive returns only when a message arrives. Both processes wait for ever. Ordering the calls differently on the two sides, or using MPI_Sendrecv, avoids it.

questions.q: How do MPI_Bcast and MPI_Scatter differ?
options: MPI_Bcast needs a reply and MPI_Scatter does not
MPI_Scatter sends to a random process
MPI_Bcast sends the same data to every process; MPI_Scatter cuts an array into pieces and gives each process one
MPI_Bcast is for numbers and MPI_Scatter for text
questions.explain: Broadcast is for what everyone needs, such as a problem size. Scatter is for sharing the work out, and MPI_Gather is its opposite.

questions.q: What is the main difference between OpenMP and MPI?
options: OpenMP is a language and MPI is an operating system
OpenMP threads share one memory inside one machine; MPI processes have separate memories and exchange messages, so they can span machines
OpenMP is for GPUs and MPI is for processors
OpenMP programs cannot have race conditions
questions.explain: Shared memory is easier to start with and exposes you to races. Message passing takes more code, has no shared variables to race on, and scales past one machine. Large codes often use both.

questions.q: What does the shuffle phase of a MapReduce job do?
options: Puts the input records in random order
Brings all the pairs with the same key together, so one reduce call sees all of that key's values
Removes repeated records
Cuts the input file into blocks
questions.explain: Map output is scattered over many machines. The shuffle sorts and routes it by key, and it is usually the most expensive part of a job, which is why combiners exist.

questions.q: When is it safe to use a job's reducer as its combiner?
options: Only when the job has a single reducer
Only when every key appears once
When combining values in separate groups and then combining the results gives the same answer, as for a sum or a maximum
Always: a combiner is only an optimisation
questions.explain: A combiner sees an arbitrary part of a key's values. A sum of sums is the sum. A mean of means is not the mean, so a mean must travel as a sum and a count.

questions.q: With as many processors as needed, how many rounds does it take to add n numbers by pairing them up?
options: About log₂ n
One
About √n
About n
questions.explain: Each round halves the number of values left. A million numbers take 20 rounds. This tree is how a reduction is done on a GPU, in MPI and in the PRAM model.

questions.q: Bisection starts from an interval of width 1. How many steps make the interval narrower than 0.001?
questions.explain: Each step halves the width, and 2¹⁰ = 1024. Bisection gains one binary digit per step: slow, and impossible to derail.

questions.q: Near a simple root, how quickly does Newton's method converge?
options: It reaches the root exactly in two steps
Linearly: one more correct digit at every step
It halves the error at every step
Quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly doubles at every step
questions.explain: The error after a step is proportional to the square of the error before it. Three or four steps from a fair guess usually reach the limit of floating point.

questions.q: Newton's method is started at a point where the derivative is almost zero. What happens?
options: The tangent is nearly flat, so the next guess lands very far away and the method may not converge
It behaves like bisection
It converges faster, because the function is nearly constant there
It stops immediately at that point
questions.explain: The update divides by the derivative. A good starting guess matters for Newton's method in a way it does not for bisection, which is why the two are often combined.

questions.q: What does the secant method use in place of the derivative in Newton's method?
options: The slope of the line through the last two guesses
A fixed slope chosen at the start
The midpoint of the last two guesses
The second derivative
questions.explain: It needs only values of the function, at the cost of converging a little more slowly than Newton's method, with order about 1.6 instead of 2.

questions.q: Doubling the number of strips in the trapezoidal rule divides its error by about
questions.explain: The error is proportional to the square of the strip width. Romberg integration uses that regularity to cancel the leading error term.

questions.q: Simpson's rule integrates polynomials exactly up to which degree?
questions.explain: It fits parabolas, so degree 2 is expected. Degree 3 comes free, because the errors on the two halves of each pair of strips cancel. Its error falls as the fourth power of the strip width.

questions.q: A Gauss-Legendre rule with n points integrates polynomials exactly up to which degree?
options: n
questions.explain: Choosing where the points go, as well as their weights, gives 2n free parameters, enough for the 2n coefficients of a polynomial of degree 2n − 1.

questions.q: The same matrix A must be used to solve Ax = b for a hundred different vectors b. What is the efficient way?
options: Factor A into L and U once, then do two triangular solves for each b
Use bisection on each equation
Compute the inverse of A a hundred times
Run Gaussian elimination from the start for each b
questions.explain: The factorisation costs about n³ operations and is done once. Each pair of triangular solves costs about n².

questions.q: Why does Gaussian elimination swap rows to bring the largest available entry to the pivot position?
options: To reduce the number of arithmetic operations
Dividing by a tiny pivot makes huge multipliers, and rounding errors are magnified
Because the method needs the rows in descending order
Because it makes the matrix symmetric
questions.explain: A pivot of exactly zero stops the method. A pivot of 1e-12 lets it continue and quietly ruins the answer. Partial pivoting keeps every multiplier at most 1.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Jacobi sweep and a Gauss-Seidel sweep?
options: Jacobi needs a symmetric matrix and Gauss-Seidel does not
Jacobi works on rows and Gauss-Seidel on columns
Jacobi computes every new value from the previous sweep; Gauss-Seidel uses each new value as soon as it has it
Jacobi is exact and Gauss-Seidel is approximate
questions.explain: Gauss-Seidel usually needs about half the sweeps. Jacobi's updates are independent of one another, so it is the one that runs naturally on a GPU.

questions.q: What property of the matrix guarantees that the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterations converge?
options: Having a determinant of 1
Having no zero entries
Having more rows than columns
Strict diagonal dominance: each diagonal entry is larger in size than the rest of its row put together
questions.explain: It is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. Symmetric positive definite matrices also make Gauss-Seidel converge.

questions.q: In successive over-relaxation, what does the factor ω do?
options: It sets the number of sweeps
It chooses which unknown is updated first
It moves each unknown past its Gauss-Seidel value; ω = 1 is plain Gauss-Seidel, and a value between 1 and 2 can converge much faster
It scales the right-hand side of the system
questions.explain: The update is x[i] += ω (new − x[i]). On the grid systems that come from differential equations, a well-chosen ω makes the number of sweeps grow in proportion to the grid size instead of its square.

questions.q: The central difference (f(x + h) − f(x − h)) / 2h has an error proportional to
options: h²
h
h³
questions.explain: The forward difference is first order, with an error proportional to h. Using a point on each side cancels that term.

questions.q: A polynomial of high degree is fitted through many equally spaced points of a smooth function and swings wildly near the ends. What is this, and what avoids it?
options: Overflow; scale the function down
Rounding error; use higher precision
Aliasing; use fewer points
Runge's phenomenon; use splines, or points crowded toward the ends such as Chebyshev points
questions.explain: More equally spaced points make it worse, not better. Low-degree pieces joined smoothly, or a better choice of points, remove the oscillation.

questions.q: What does a cubic spline guarantee where two of its pieces meet?
options: Only the value agrees
The value, the first derivative and the second derivative all agree
The two pieces are the same cubic
The value and the third derivative agree
questions.explain: That smoothness is why a spline looks like one curve. Each piece is its own cubic, and the matching conditions lead to a tridiagonal system, which is cheap to solve.

questions.q: What is catastrophic cancellation?
options: Subtracting two nearly equal numbers, which leaves few correct digits
Dividing by a number close to zero
Adding numbers until the result overflows
Two rounding errors that cancel exactly
questions.explain: If two values agree in their first ten digits, their difference keeps only the digits after that. It is why a finite difference stops improving when the step becomes too small.

questions.q: A Markov chain has transition matrix P. Where are the probabilities of going from state i to state j in exactly n steps?
options: In row j, column i of P
In row i, column j of n times P
In row i, column j of P multiplied by itself n times
They cannot be found without simulating the chain
questions.explain: This is the content of the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations: the routes from i to j in m + n steps go through some state k after m steps, which is matrix multiplication written out.

questions.q: When is a distribution π stationary for a chain with transition matrix P?
options: When one more step leaves it unchanged: πP = π
When every state has the same probability
When P multiplied by π gives zero
When the chain has stopped moving
questions.explain: The chain keeps moving; only the probabilities stop changing. π is a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1.

questions.q: A machine that works today is broken tomorrow with probability 0.1. A broken one is repaired by tomorrow with probability 0.5. In the long run, on what fraction of days does it work?
questions.explain: In the steady state the flow out of 'working' equals the flow in: 0.1 π(working) = 0.5 π(broken). So working is five times as likely as broken.

questions.q: What makes a finite Markov chain settle to the same stationary distribution from every starting state?
options: Having at least one state that is never left
Having equal probabilities in every row
Having a symmetric transition matrix
Being irreducible and aperiodic: every state can reach every other, and returns are not locked to a fixed cycle
questions.explain: A chain that splits into separate parts has several stationary distributions. One that cycles has one, but never settles into it. PageRank adds random jumps to guarantee both properties.

questions.q: Requests arrive as a Poisson process at a rate of 3 a minute. What is the probability that no request arrives in a given minute?
options: e⁻³, about 0.05
questions.explain: The number of arrivals in time t is Poisson with mean λt, so the probability of none is e^(−λt).

questions.q: In a Poisson process with rate λ, what distribution do the gaps between arrivals follow?
options: Uniform between 0 and 1/λ
Normal, with mean λ
Exponential, with mean 1/λ
Poisson, with mean λ
questions.explain: Counting arrivals gives the Poisson distribution; timing the gaps gives the exponential. They are two views of the same process.

questions.q: Buses arrive as a Poisson process, on average one every 10 minutes. You have already waited 5 minutes. How much longer do you expect to wait?
options: 5 minutes
10 minutes
15 minutes
2.5 minutes
questions.explain: The exponential distribution has no memory: the time already waited tells nothing about the time left. It is the only continuous distribution with this property.

questions.q: A server can handle 10 requests a second on average, and 8 arrive. In the M/M/1 model, what is the mean number of requests in the system?
questions.explain: Utilisation ρ is 8/10 = 0.8, and the mean number in the system is ρ / (1 − ρ) = 4. At ρ = 0.9 it would be 9.

questions.q: The load on an M/M/1 queue rises from 90% to 99% of the server's capacity. What happens to the mean time a request spends in the system?
options: It doubles
It stays the same until the load passes 100%
It becomes about ten times longer
It rises by about 9%
questions.explain: The mean time is 1 / (μ − λ). The gap μ − λ shrinks from a tenth of capacity to a hundredth. Delay explodes as utilisation nears 1, which is why servers are run well below full load.

questions.q: What does Little's law say?
options: The mean wait equals the service time divided by the number of servers
Arrivals and departures are equal at every instant
The mean number in a system equals the arrival rate times the mean time spent in it: L = λW
A queue is stable only if it is empty half the time
questions.explain: It holds for any system in steady state, whatever the distributions. If 8 requests a second arrive and each stays half a second, 4 are present on average.

questions.q: In the notation M/M/s for a queue, what do the three parts mean?
options: Mean arrival rate, mean service rate, and system size
Minimum, maximum and steady-state queue length
Markov chain, memory size, and number of states
Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, and s servers
questions.explain: M stands for Markov, or memoryless. M/M/1 is the single-server case. A G in place of an M means a general distribution.

questions.q: In a birth and death process, to which states can the process move from state n?
options: Only to state 0
To any state
Only to n + 1 or n − 1
Only to n + 1
questions.explain: One arrival or one departure at a time. Queues are the standard example, and the restriction is what makes their steady-state equations solvable by balancing the flow between neighbours.

questions.q: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n describes merge sort. What does it solve to?
options: Θ(log n)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
Θ(n²)
questions.explain: There are log n levels of halving, and each level does n work in total. The master theorem gives the same answer: the work is spread evenly over the levels.

questions.q: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n describes quicksort when the pivot is always the smallest value. What does it solve to?
options: Θ(n²)
Θ(2ⁿ)
Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.explain: The work is n + (n − 1) + ... + 1, about n²/2. A pivot from the middle, or a random one, makes this case unlikely.

questions.q: What dominates the running time of Kruskal's algorithm on a graph with E edges?
options: Visiting every pair of nodes: O(V²)
The union-find operations: O(E × V)
Sorting the edges: O(E log E)
Finding the cheapest edge E times: O(E²)
questions.explain: With path compression each union-find operation is close to constant time, so the sort is the expensive step.

questions.q: What does the Floyd-Warshall algorithm cost on a graph with V nodes?
options: O(V²) time and O(V) memory
O(V² log V) time and O(V²) memory
O(V³) time and O(V²) memory
O(V × E) time and O(V) memory
questions.explain: Three nested loops over the nodes, and a table with one entry for each pair. The cost does not depend on the number of edges, so it suits dense graphs.

questions.q: A matrix with n rows has k non-zero entries. About how many numbers does compressed sparse row storage keep?
options: 3k × n
n × n
2k + n
k
questions.explain: One value and one column number for each non-zero entry, and one pointer for each row plus one. For a million rows with five entries each that is 11 million numbers instead of 10¹².

questions.q: A has the singular value decomposition UΣVᵀ. How are its singular values related to AᵀA?
options: They are the eigenvalues of AᵀA
They are unrelated to AᵀA
They are the diagonal entries of AᵀA
They are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA
questions.explain: AᵀA = VΣ²Vᵀ, so the columns of V are its eigenvectors and the squared singular values are its eigenvalues.

questions.q: How is the best rank-k approximation of a matrix obtained, in the least-squares sense?
options: Keep the k largest singular values and their singular vectors, and drop the rest
Keep the first k rows
Keep the k columns with the largest norms
Set the k smallest entries to zero
questions.explain: This is the Eckart-Young theorem. It is why truncating an SVD compresses a matrix, and what PCA does to centred data.

questions.q: A vector is multiplied by a matrix A again and again and rescaled each time. What does it converge to?
options: The first column of A
The eigenvector whose eigenvalue is smallest
The eigenvector whose eigenvalue is largest in magnitude
The zero vector
questions.explain: This is power iteration. Its speed depends on the ratio between the two largest eigenvalues, and it is the method behind PageRank.

questions.q: In a space of very many dimensions, where is most of the volume of a ball?
options: On one axis
Spread evenly along every radius
In a thin shell just inside its surface
Near its centre
questions.explain: Volume grows as the radius to the power d. For large d, shrinking the radius by 1% already removes most of the volume. Nearest-neighbour methods suffer because almost all points end up nearly equally far apart.

questions.q: What does the central limit theorem say about the mean of many independent samples from one distribution?
options: It has the same distribution as a single sample
It equals the true mean exactly
It is uniformly distributed
It is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the original distribution
questions.explain: The original distribution needs a finite variance. The spread of the mean shrinks like 1/√n, which is why averaging more samples gives slowly diminishing returns.

questions.q: X is never negative and has a mean of 10. What does Markov's inequality say about the probability that X is at least 100?
options: It is at most 0.1
It is at least 0.1
It is exactly 0.1
It is at most 0.01
questions.explain: P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a. It uses nothing but the mean, so it is weak, and it is the starting point for every stronger tail bound.

questions.q: A variable has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. By Chebyshev's inequality, the probability of being 20 or more away from the mean is at most
questions.explain: P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k². Twenty is four standard deviations, so the bound is 1/16, for any distribution with that mean and variance.

questions.q: For the sum of many independent coin flips, why is a Chernoff bound more useful than Chebyshev's inequality?
options: It gives the exact probability
It needs no assumption of independence
It applies to a single flip
Its bound on a large deviation shrinks exponentially with the number of flips, not just like 1/n
questions.explain: Independence is what buys the exponential decay. It is the tool behind statements such as 'with a thousand samples the estimate is within 5% with probability 99.9%'.

questions.q: Linear discriminant analysis and PCA both project data to fewer dimensions. What is the difference?
options: PCA needs labels and LDA does not
LDA keeps every dimension and PCA drops some
LDA uses the class labels and looks for directions that separate the classes; PCA ignores labels and looks for the most variance
LDA is for images and PCA for text
questions.explain: The direction of largest variance need not be the one that tells the classes apart. LDA maximises the spread between class means relative to the spread within each class.

questions.q: How does a maximum a posteriori estimate differ from a maximum likelihood estimate?
options: It also weighs a prior belief about the parameters; with a Gaussian prior on the weights it becomes L2 regularisation
It uses the test set as well as the training set
It is the same estimate computed on more data
It always gives a larger likelihood
questions.explain: Maximum likelihood asks which parameters make the data most probable. MAP multiplies that by the prior. The log of a Gaussian prior is a penalty on the squared weights.
